title: Carved apple-wood dessert fork
subtitle: Green-wood spoon-carving: a two-tine fork from apple branch
excerpt: A small two-tine dessert fork carved from a fresh apple or crab-apple branch. Apple carves cleanly, dries without checking if the walls are even, and takes a warm honey-red finish under linseed oil. The tines are cut with a coping saw, then refined with knife and sandpaper.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the spoon-fork progression; Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861) chapter on table woodwork for the tine proportions.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves under hand tools without the resistance of dry timber.
The rough-shaped piece of wood before fine carving begins.
A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the Swedish school-craft standard for whittling and spoon-carving.

content.text: An apple-wood dessert fork is a small two-tine fork for fruit, cake, and cheese. Apple wood is dense, fine-grained, and cuts cleanly in both directions with a sharp sloyd knife. The tines are sawn in with a coping saw before the final shaping, which avoids the difficulty of trying to split them by knife alone. This is a good intermediate step after a first jam spoon: the plan shape is familiar, but the tine-cutting adds a new step.
This project uses
green wood
. Apple from a pruned orchard branch works well. The branch should be at least 3 cm across so there is enough width for both tines side by side.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
What you need
Wood
One straight-grained apple or crab-apple
blank

cut from a pruning, roughly 18 cm long and at least 3 cm in diameter. Split along the pith to give a flat working face. Apple is food-safe under a drying oil and turns warm gold-to-brown with age. Cherry is a good alternative: similar density, slightly paler. Birch works but is softer and the tines need extra care not to snap.
Tools
Sloyd knife for shaping the handle and tine profile.
Coping saw for cutting the tine slots.
Hook knife, small, for any bowl-cleaning at the tine base.
Leather strop.
180-grit and 240-grit sandpaper for tine edges.
Raw linseed oil.
Workspace

A low carving stool or a workbench at a comfortable seated height. The coping-saw cuts need the blank held firmly, a carver's vice, a clamp to the bench edge, or the knee-brace grip described in Step 4 below.
The work
Step 1: Mark the profile

Draw the fork on the flat face of the blank. The overall length is about 17 cm. The tine section is 5 cm long; the handle 12 cm. Mark two tines, each about 8 mm wide, separated by a 6 mm slot. The base of the tines (the widest point of the head) is 22 mm across, the two tines plus the slot.
Step 2: Rough out the plan shape
Use
push cuts
with the
sloyd knife
to remove waste from the sides of the handle and the outside of the tine head. Work to the pencil line but leave 1, 2 mm of extra material, the final shaping comes after the tine slot is cut.
Step 3: Cut the back profile and depth

Turn the blank over. Use push cuts to thin the tine section from the back until the tine head is about 5 mm thick. The handle taper starts here: it should be 10, 12 mm thick at the shoulder and thin to 7, 8 mm at the end. The junction between handle and tine head needs a
stop cut
across the grain on both sides of the shoulder before you cut toward it from the handle, this prevents the grain tearing through the tine section.
Step 4: Saw the tine slot

Clamp the blank to a bench edge or hold it in a knee-brace (the blank braced flat on your thigh, your non-dominant hand pressing it steady, the coping saw in your dominant hand). Saw along the centreline of the tine slot, starting from the tip and sawing down to the marked base line, about 5 cm. Saw slowly and keep the blade vertical. If the slot wanders, work the tines apart with the blade before continuing. Stop the saw cut at the base line; do not saw past it.
Step 5: Refine the tines

Use push cuts with the sloyd knife to taper the outside edges of each tine so they narrow slightly toward the tip. Each tine should be about 6 mm wide at the base and 4 mm at the tip. Round the tip of each tine with short thumb-pivot cuts. The inner faces of the tines (the slot walls) get folded 180-grit sandpaper run down them to smooth the saw kerf, the sloyd knife cannot reach these faces cleanly.
Step 6: Final shaping and surface

Use push cuts to refine the back curve of the tine section and the handle. A light pass with 240-grit sandpaper along the outside surfaces brings everything to a consistent finish. Keep tool marks on the handle, they read as hand-made, which is the point.
Finishing

Let the fork dry for two days before finishing. Apply raw linseed oil to all surfaces including inside the tine slot. Let soak for one hour, wipe off the surplus. Re-apply after twenty-four hours. Cure for two weeks before food contact. Apple wood takes raw linseed oil readily and deepens to a warm amber over the first few applications.
Variations
Three-tine version: same slot cut twice, producing three tines each 6 mm wide separated by two 5 mm slots. Requires the tine section to be at least 28 mm wide, use a branch with a larger diameter.
Cherry or pear: both denser than apple, slightly harder to carve, but take a finer finished edge. Cherry darkens over time.
Left-handed: the fork is symmetrical; no adjustment is needed for a left-handed user.
Care
Hand wash only. Dry immediately and re-oil when the wood looks pale. Do not soak and do not put in a dishwasher.

attrs.symptom: One tine snaps when refining with the knife
attrs.cause: Tine too thin, or a cut was made against the grain at the tine tip
attrs.fix: Work only with the grain along the length of the tine, push cuts from base to tip on the outside, never from tip toward base on the outside. If a tine cracks, carve back to a clean two-tine fork or recut as a single-tine skewer.

attrs.symptom: The coping saw wanders off-centre in the slot
attrs.cause: Sawing too fast, or the blank is not held still
attrs.fix: Slow the stroke and clamp the blank properly. If the slot is off-centre, file the wider half back with a small round file or folded sandpaper before refining the tines.

attrs.symptom: The grain tears at the shoulder between handle and tines
attrs.cause: No stop cut was made at the base of the tine section before cutting toward it
attrs.fix: Make the stop cut first, a short vertical cut straight across the grain at the base line, before any cuts that travel toward it. This sets the grain break at the right point.
